title: POSE — Object-Oriented Programming in C#
text:
Introduction
This book collects the course material of POSE — Object-Oriented Programming in C# for class 2AHIF at HTL Leonding, school year 2026/27. It grows over the year, one part per unit. Each part holds the theory of its unit and the live demos from class.
The exercises are not part of the book: you get them through Classroom50.

title: OO Basics
text:
NoteWhy object orientation?



Object-oriented programming is the foundation most modern software is built on, because organizing code around objects that bundle data and behavior together is what makes large, evolving systems stay manageable.


This unit introduces classes and objects in C#, using a Pupil class as the running example. The theory is split into these chapters:

From Structured to Object-Oriented: what objects are and why we use them
Classes and Objects: defining a class, fields, and creating objects with new
Constructors: bringing a new object into a working state
Properties in Detail: auto, computed and fully written-out properties
Static vs. Instance: members shared by all objects of a class, and const vs. readonly vs. static
Enumerations: named constant values with enum
Naming Conventions: how to name classes, properties, fields and methods
UML Class and Object Diagrams: the PlantUML notation used in the exercises, and snapshots of the objects at runtime
Glossary: the most important terms of this unit

title: 1  From Structured to Object-Oriented
text:
1.1 Goals of OO
In the first year you wrote structured (procedural) programs:
This works well for small programs. In larger ones, data and the methods working on it drift apart, and it gets hard to see who is allowed to change what.
Object-oriented programming (OO) puts data and logic back together: an object holds its data and the methods that work on that data. Each object is responsible for one part of the overall task.

title: 1  From Structured to Object-Oriented
text:
Reusability: an object is a self-contained building block that can be used in many places.

Single Responsibility Principle: a class should have exactly one responsibility.

Encapsulation: how an object works is hidden inside. Other code only uses its public interface (a “contract”), so the inside can change without breaking the outside.
Testability and extensibility: a defined interface is easy to test, and an object can later get new capabilities.

title: 1  From Structured to Object-Oriented
text:
1.2 What Is an Object?
An object has two sides that only make sense together:

State: its data. A pupil has a first name, last name, date of birth and ZIP code.
Behavior: its methods. A pupil can tell whether it is of full age, whether it is older than another pupil, or whether it lives nearby.







ImportantObject = state + behavior



Behavior uses the state and may change it, and the state influences the result of the behavior. Only together do they make up an object.


The blueprint for objects is a class. It is similar to a record, but contains not only data, it also contains behavior.

title: 1  From Structured to Object-Oriented
text:
1.3 Finding Classes
To design an object-oriented program, read the task description and look for the important nouns: they are candidates for classes. Then decide which data each class needs (state) and what it must be able to do (behavior).
Example: for a school administration, Pupil is an obvious class:



State (fields)
Behavior (methods)




FirstName, LastName
IsOfFullAge


DateOfBirth
IsOlderThan


ZipCode, City
LivesNearby



The next chapter turns this into C# code.

title: 2  Classes and Objects
text:
2.1 Classes Are Blueprints for Objects
A class describes what objects of a certain kind look like and what they can do. It is one level of structure above a method: where a method bundles a few statements into one task, a class bundles data and several methods into one unit.
A class defines three things:
As a rule of thumb, data is private and is reached from the outside through properties, while the methods that form the object’s “interface” are public. Methods that only help other methods of the class do their work stay private.

title: 2  Classes and Objects
2  Classes and Objects
text:
2.2 Classes Are Templates
Think of a class as a stamp. The Pupil stamp has the fields FirstName, LastName, DateOfBirth and ZipCode, and the methods IsOfAge, IsOlderThan and LivesNearby. With this one stamp you can create as many pupil objects as you like. Each has its own, independent values (one pupil named Max Muster with ZIP 4060, another named Erika Musterfrau with ZIP 1010), and each can run the same methods on its own data.

title: 2  Classes and Objects
section: 2.3 Instantiation: Creating Objects Based on Classes
text:
2.3 Instantiation: Creating Objects Based on Classes
Creating an object from a class is called instantiation, and the object is called an instance of the class. The Pupil class defines the structure (FirstName, LastName, DateOfBirth, ZipCode, …), and each instance fills it with its own values:



FirstName
LastName
DateOfBirth
ZipCode




Anna
Müller
2008-05-12
4060


Paul
Gruber
2006-07-30
(none)



The chapter UML Class and Object Diagrams shows how to draw such objects.

2.3.1 Creating and Using Objects
In code, objects are created with the new operator:
Pupil pupil = new Pupil();

pupil.FirstName = "Max";
pupil.LastName = "Muster";

Console.WriteLine($"{pupil.FirstName,-15} {pupil.LastName,-35}");
Here is what happens step by step:

new Pupil() reserves memory for a new object on the heap, the memory area for objects. A class is always a reference type.
new returns a reference to that object, a kind of address that says where it lives in memory. The variable pupil stores this reference, not the object itself.
With the dot operator (pupil.FirstName) you reach the properties and methods of exactly the object the variable refers to.







WarningNo object, no access



You can only use an object after it has been created. If a variable of type Pupil does not refer to any object yet (its value is null), pupil.FirstName fails at runtime with a NullReferenceException.


Since C# 9 you can omit the class name after new when the compiler already knows the type from the left side. This is called target-typed new:
Pupil pupil = new();


2.3.2 The Relationship Between Object and Class
Class and object are easy to mix up, so here is how they differ:







Class
Object




Exists exactly once in the program
There can be any number of them


Describes what objects look like (state, behavior)
Holds concrete values and executes the operations


Is fixed when you write the code
Is created (and removed) while the program runs


Blueprint for creating objects
Built from that blueprint



Each object is an instance of its class:
Class  <┄┄instance of┄┄  Object


2.3.3 Methods
So far the pupil only holds data. Methods add behavior: they describe what an object can do. A method of a class can read the object’s data and can also change it, e.g. a method Move() of a horse could increase its position. In a class diagram, the methods are listed in a second section below the data:

You already know how to write methods from the first year. The only difference is that these methods don’t need the pupil’s data as parameters: they belong to the object and can use its fields and properties directly.

title: 3  Constructors
text:
3.1 Constructor ➔ Hooking into Instantiation
In the previous chapter, a pupil was created in two steps: first new Pupil(), then setting the properties one by one. That has a weakness: between these steps the object exists, but it is incomplete. Forget one assignment, and you have a pupil without a last name. A constructor solves this. It is special code that runs automatically while an object is being created, so the object is complete from its very first moment.
Syntax
A constructor looks like a method, with two differences:
A class can have several constructors with different parameter lists (overloading, see below).
If you don’t write any constructor, C# creates a default constructor for you. It has no parameters and does nothing. That is why new Pupil() worked in the previous chapter.
Purpose
The constructor’s job is to bring a new object into a working state, so that it can fulfill its purpose right away. To do this, it initializes the fields. It often takes parameters for the data an object cannot do without. A pupil without a name or a date of birth makes no sense, so the constructor demands them.

title: 3  Constructors
text:
It is named exactly like the class (Pupil).
It has no return type, not even void. It doesn’t return anything, because new already delivers the new object.

section: 3.2 Instead of new and Set… ➔ Constructor

title: 3  Constructors
4  Properties in Detail
text:
4.1 Automatic Properties
From the outside, a property looks like a variable of the object: you read and assign it with the dot operator. On the inside, however, it consists of two small pieces of code, the accessors. get runs when the value is read, and set runs when a value is assigned. The set accessor receives the new value in a hidden parameter called value.
C# offers several ways to write a property, from a one-liner to a full block of code. This chapter shows them one after the other, and each time explains which problem the longer form solves. At the end, a table sums up which form to use when.
Most properties just store a value and hand it back. For them, the shortest form is enough, the automatic property (auto property). You only write the data type, the name, and which accessors exist:
Using the property looks like using a variable:
The value has to be stored somewhere. For an auto property, the compiler secretly creates a private field for it, the backing field, and fills in the accessor code. So the one-liner above behaves like this longer code:
This is why a property is often called a public wrapper around a field: the field stores the value, and the property controls how it is read and written. Not every field needs a property, though. Data that is only used inside the class stays a plain private field.

title: 4  Properties in Detail
4  Properties in Detail
4  Properties in Detail
4  Properties in Detail
text:
4.6 Handling Invalid Values
What should a setter do when value fails the check? There are three options, each with an advantage and a drawback:

Don’t set it at all: the object never gets an incorrect value, but the caller doesn’t learn that something went wrong.
Throw an exception: the object never gets an incorrect value and the caller is notified, but the program stops unless the caller handles the exception. You will learn about exceptions later in the year.
Set a meaningful default value instead: the object never gets an incorrect value and the program keeps working, but the caller gets no feedback about the invalid value.

Which option fits best is up to the author of the class and depends on the specific value and on what the program is for. Pupil.ZipCode uses option 1: an invalid ZIP code is simply ignored, as the exercise requires.






TipUse the properties inside the class, too



The class itself should use its properties as well, instead of accessing a backing field directly, even if that means working with a private setter. Otherwise a constructor could write _zipCode = 42; and bypass the check in the setter. When all code goes through the property, the checks always run and are written in one place only. With field this happens automatically, because there is no named backing field to write to.

title: 5  Static vs. Instance
text:
5.1 Fields
So far, everything in a class belonged to the individual objects: every pupil has its own first name, its own date of birth, its own ZIP code. Members like these are called instance members, and they remain the normal case.
Sometimes, however, a value belongs to the class as a whole rather than to one object. The 01-Pupils exercise has such a case: every pupil gets a unique, ever-increasing Id. To hand out the next id, somebody has to remember which id comes next. That counter can’t be stored in each pupil, because every pupil would have its own copy and they would all start at the same number. It must exist once for the whole class. Members like that are marked with the keyword static.
A static field exists exactly once, no matter how many objects there are, and all instances share it. When one pupil changes it, all other pupils see the new value:
Every time a new Pupil is created, the constructor copies the shared _nextId into the pupil’s own Id, then increases the counter for the next pupil. The first pupil gets id 1, the second id 2, and so on. That’s why _nextId must be static, while Id is a normal instance property: every pupil has its own id, but they all share one counter.

title: 5  Static vs. Instance
5  Static vs. Instance
text:
5.2 Methods
Methods can be static, too. A static method belongs to the class, not to an object, so it runs without any instance. That’s why you call it via the class name: Console.WriteLine(...) and Math.Max(...) are static methods, and so were all the methods you wrote in the first year.
This has a few consequences:

A static method cannot use instance fields or properties, and cannot use this: there is no “current object” whose data it could access. It can use static fields.
Its only way to work with objects is to receive them as parameters.
Apart from that it’s a normal method: it can be overloaded, and access modifiers like public and private apply as usual.

Although static methods belong to the class, good static methods are the opposite of side-effect-prone code. They work only with their parameters and return a result, without keeping any data between calls. We call such methods stateless. They are easy to understand and easy to test, which is why they were all you needed in the first year. If a method doesn’t use any instance data, the IDE often suggests making it static.

title: 5  Static vs. Instance
text:
5.3 Static Class
If a class contains only static members, you can declare the class itself as static class. This is typical for a collection of helper methods that don’t need any state. The best-known example is System.Math: Math.Sqrt, Math.Round and Math.Max are all static, and a “math object” would make no sense.






Note



You cannot create an instance of a static class. new Math() does not compile.

title: 5  Static vs. Instance
text:
5.4 const, readonly and static Compared
Three keywords change how a field behaves, and they are easy to mix up: const, readonly and static. They answer two different questions:

How many copies exist? One per object (instance field), or one for the whole class (static, and every const).
When can the value change? Never, because it is fixed in the code (const); once, in the constructor (readonly); or any time (neither).

This HorseRace class uses all of them:
public class HorseRace
{
    public const int MaxSteps = 20;
    public static readonly DateTime StartTime = DateTime.Now;
    private static int _raceCount;
    private readonly Horse[] _horses;

    public HorseRace(Horse[] horses)
    {
        _horses = horses;
        _raceCount++;
    }
}
const: a constant, fixed when you write the code. MaxSteps is 20 in every race and in every run of the program. The compiler writes the value directly into every place where MaxSteps is used, so it must be known at compile time: a number, a bool, a char or a string literal. DateTime.Now or new Horse[5] are not possible. A constant belongs to the class, not to an object, so you use it via the class name: HorseRace.MaxSteps. It is automatically static, and writing static const is even a compile error.
readonly: set once, then fixed. _horses gets its value in the constructor, and after that nobody can assign a different array to it, not even the class itself (_horses = ...; in a method is a compile error). Unlike a constant, the value is only known at runtime: each race gets the horses that are passed to its constructor. So every object has its own readonly value.
static: one copy for the whole class. _raceCount exists once and counts all races ever created. Without readonly, it can change at any time, with the side effects described above.
static readonly: one copy, set once at runtime. StartTime exists once for the whole class and never changes, but its value is only known when the program runs, so it can’t be a const. Use static readonly for constants that the compiler can’t compute: a DateTime, an array, an object.










Keyword

Example

static

const

To choose, ask the two questions from above:

Is the value the same for every object and known when you write the code? Use const.
Is it the same for every object, but only known at runtime? Use static readonly.
Does each object get its own value that never changes after the constructor? Use readonly.
Does the value change while the program runs? Leave readonly out, and add static only if all objects must share it.







Warningreadonly protects the reference, not the object



For an array or another object, readonly only means that the field always refers to the same array. The contents can still change: _horses[0] = new Horse("Lara"); compiles and replaces the first horse, and sorting the array rearranges its elements. readonly prevents only _horses = new Horse[3];.


For properties, the same idea is called a get-only property (public int Age { get; }, see Properties in Detail): like a readonly field, it can only be assigned in the constructor.

title: 6  Enumerations (enum)
text:
You have already used an enum now and then, e.g. ConsoleColor.Red or ConsoleKey.Enter. Now it’s time to understand what an enum actually is.
Often a value can only take a few fixed options: a traffic light is red, yellow or green, and a pupil can be checked against voting age, full age or retirement age. You could encode such options as numbers (0 = voting age, 1 = full age, …) or as strings. However, numbers mean nothing to the reader, and a typo in a string is only noticed when the program runs. An enumeration gives each option a name that the compiler knows and checks.
An enum is a data type that consists of a fixed list of named constants. The 01-Pupils exercise needs one for AgeType:
enum AgeType
{
    VotingAge, // 0
    FullAge, // 1
    RetirementAge // 2
}
A variable of type AgeType can only hold one of these three values. If you write AgeType.FulAge, the compiler reports the typo immediately.
Behind the scenes, every entry is a unique number of an integer type. By default it’s int, and that’s fine: byte, short and long are also possible, but they only matter in special cases such as talking to hardware or code written in other languages. Unless you say otherwise, the entries are numbered 0, 1, 2, … in the order they appear in the code, as the comments above show.
This is how you work with an enum:
AgeType type = AgeType.FullAge;
Console.WriteLine(type); // Output: FullAge

type = (AgeType)2;
Console.WriteLine(type); // Output: RetirementAge

int value = (int)AgeType.VotingAge;
Console.WriteLine(value); // Output: 0

type = Enum.Parse<AgeType>("FullAge"); // TryParse would be the smarter choice
Console.WriteLine(type); // Output: FullAge
Line by line:

An entry is always written with the type name in front: AgeType.FullAge. Console.WriteLine prints its name, not its number.
A cast converts in both directions: (AgeType)2 turns the number 2 into RetirementAge, and (int)AgeType.VotingAge gives the number 0.
Enum.Parse<AgeType>("FullAge") turns a string, e.g. read from a file, into the matching entry. It throws an exception if the string doesn’t match any entry. That’s why Enum.TryParse is the better choice, following the same TryParse pattern you know from int.TryParse.

You can also assign the numbers yourself, e.g. FullAge = 18. Usually the default numbering is fine, and it’s all AgeType needs here.
Check your understanding of this chapter with the Enumerations Self-Check Quiz.

title: 7  Naming Conventions
text:
7.1 How Names Are Written
The compiler doesn’t care whether a property is called FirstName, firstname or fn. People do. Code is read far more often than it is written, and names are what a reader sees first. C# developers all over the world follow the same naming conventions, based on Microsoft’s guidelines. If you follow them too, anyone can tell at a glance whether a name is a class, a property, a field or a local variable, without scrolling to its declaration.
The conventions answer two questions: how a name is written (upper- or lowercase, underscore) and what a name should say.
C# uses two styles of capitalization:
Neither style uses spaces or underscores between words. The only underscore is the prefix of private fields.
The rule of thumb: everything that is visible from outside a class (the class itself, its public properties, methods and constants) is written in PascalCase. Everything that is local or private data (parameters, local variables, private fields) starts with a lowercase letter, and private fields additionally get a leading underscore. The one exception: constants are always PascalCase, even when they are private (DelayMilliseconds in HorseRace).
The different styles also help where names are similar: a parameter name, a field _name and a property Name can exist side by side in one class, and you always know which one is meant.

title: 7  Naming Conventions
text:
PascalCase: every word starts with an uppercase letter, including the first: Pupil, FirstName, IsOlderThan, HorseRace.
camelCase: like PascalCase, but the first letter is lowercase: firstName, dateOfBirth, startNumber.

The exercises ship an .editorconfig file with exactly these rules. Rider and Visual Studio underline names that break them and suggest a fix. The build still succeeds, so it’s up to you: fix these hints right away instead of ignoring them.

title: 7  Naming Conventions
text:
7.2 What Names Should Say
A correctly capitalized name can still be a bad name. These guidelines help you choose good ones:

Classes are nouns, in the singular: Pupil, Horse, HorseRace. An object of the class is one such thing. A class name like Pupils or ManagePupils is a hint that something is wrong.
Methods are verbs, because they do something: Move(), PrintResults(), AssignRanks(). A method that answers a yes/no question starts with Is, Has or Can and returns bool: IsOlderThan(other), IsOfAge(type).
Properties are nouns or adjectives, because they describe the object: FirstName, Age, Position. A bool property also starts with Is, Has or Can: IsFinished, HasZipCode.
Collections are plural: an array of horses is called _horses, not _horse or _horseArray.
Say what it is, not how it is stored: DateOfBirth, not DateString or Dob.
No abbreviations unless everybody knows them (Id, Html). Autocompletion writes long names for you, so startNumber costs nothing compared to sn.
English only: C# keywords and the .NET class library are English, so Pupil.IsOfAge reads naturally, while a mix like Schueler.IsVolljaehrig does not.
One class per file, and the file has the same name as the class: Pupil lives in Pupil.cs.







TipRenaming is cheap



If you notice that a name no longer fits, rename it with your IDE’s rename refactoring (Rename in the context menu; Ctrl+R, R in Visual Studio, Ctrl+R, R or Shift+F6 in Rider, depending on its keymap). It updates every usage in the whole solution, so there is no excuse for keeping a misleading name.

title: 8  UML Class and Object Diagrams
text:
8.1 Class Diagrams
UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standardized set of diagram types for describing software design independently of any programming language. The class diagram is UML’s diagram for static structure: it shows the classes in a system, their members (fields, properties, methods), and how classes relate to one another — without any of the runtime behavior or control flow.
PlantUML is a text-based way to author UML diagrams: you write the diagram as plain text (@startuml … @enduml), and a renderer turns it into an image. See the class diagram and object diagram syntax references for the full notation.
This chapter covers two UML diagram types: class diagrams show the blueprint of the classes, object diagrams show the objects that exist at one moment while the program runs.

NoteWhy class diagrams matter



Class diagrams matter in software development because they let you communicate and review a design before (or without) reading all the code: given a class’s public members and its relationships to other classes, another developer can understand what it’s responsible for and how to use it.

title: 8  UML Class and Object Diagrams
text:
8.2 Object Diagrams
A class diagram shows the blueprint: which data and methods every object of a class has. An object diagram shows what exists at one particular moment while the program runs: the concrete objects, the values of their data, and which objects refer to which. You can think of it as a snapshot of the heap.






NoteWhy object diagrams matter



Object diagrams matter because many bugs are not about what a class looks like, but about which objects exist at runtime and how they are connected: drawing the objects step by step lets you follow a program the way you did desk checks in the first year, and see mistakes such as a missing object or a reference to the wrong one.


An object diagram differs from a class diagram in a few ways:

Concrete values instead of types: a class diagram says +string FirstName, an object diagram says FirstName = "Anna". All data of the object is shown, including private fields, because it all belongs to the object’s state.
No methods: all objects of a class have the same methods, so they would add nothing to the snapshot.
No static fields: they belong to the class, not to an object. Pupil._nextId therefore never appears in an object box.
Many boxes per class: there is one box per object, so a class can appear many times, or not at all if no object of it exists at that moment.


8.2.1 Object Diagram Notation








Symbol
Meaning
Rendered As




object "name : Class" as alias
an object named name of class Class
a box with name : Class as heading


__text__
underlined text
UML underlines object headings to tell them apart from classes


": Class" (no name)
an anonymous object
heading shows only : Class, e.g. an array element


name = value
current value of a field or property
plain line in the box, e.g. ZipCode = 4060


a --> b : label
link: a holds a reference to b
solid arrow, labeled with the field that holds the reference


allowmixing
classes and objects in the same diagram
lets class boxes appear next to object boxes


a ..> Class : <<instanceOf>>
a is an instance of Class
dashed arrow labeled «instanceOf»



The alias is only used inside the PlantUML text to draw links (anna, race). It is not shown in the diagram.


8.2.2 Illustration: Two Pupil Objects
The two pupils from the chapter Classes and Objects as an object diagram. Each object has its own values, and both are instances of the same class. paul was created without a ZIP code, so his _zipCode is null.

Same diagram, as plain text (for reference — this block isn’t rendered):
@startuml
allowmixing

class Pupil {
    -DateOnly _dateOfBirth [readonly]
    -int? _zipCode
    +int Id [readonly]
    +string FirstName [readonly]
    +string LastName [readonly]
}
object "__anna : Pupil__" as anna {
    Id = 1
    FirstName = "Anna"
    LastName = "Müller"
    _dateOfBirth = 2008-05-12
    _zipCode = 4060
}
object "__paul : Pupil__" as paul {
    Id = 2
    FirstName = "Paul"
    LastName = "Gruber"
    _dateOfBirth = 2006-07-30
    _zipCode = null
}
anna ..> Pupil : <<instanceOf>>
paul ..> Pupil : <<instanceOf>>

@enduml


8.2.3 Illustration: Objects That Refer to Each Other
Object diagrams really pay off when objects hold references to other objects. In the 03-HorseRace exercise, a HorseRace object keeps its horses in the array _horses. This snapshot shows a race with three horses in the middle of a run:

Each arrow is one element of the array: _horses[0] holds a reference to egon, and so on. The horses themselves don’t know the race, so there are no arrows back. After the next MoveHorses() call, the Position values change, but the arrows stay the same. A second snapshot would show exactly that.

title: 9  Glossary
text:
Term
Description
Syntax




Class
Data type, blueprint, template
public class Pupil {}


Object
Instance, object instance, concrete manifestation of a class
Pupil p = new Pupil();


Object diagram
UML diagram that shows the objects existing at one moment at runtime, with their current values and the references between them.
object "__anna : Pupil__" as anna { ... } (PlantUML)


Object reference
Variable of the class’s type that points to a concrete object instance (or null). The variable lives on the stack and holds the memory address of the object on the heap (or null).
Pupil p;
p = new Pupil();
p = null;


Constructor
Method that is called with new while an object is being instantiated (created).
Method with no return value, method name == class name


Default constructor
A parameterless constructor exists automatically, unless you define a custom constructor.
public Pupil(){}


Custom constructor
Used to shape/initialize the new object with specific parameters. This is how, e.g., mandatory properties of an object are established at the very start of its lifetime. Example: Pupil p = new Pupil("Susi", "Huber");
public Pupil(string firstName, string LastName) {}


Properties
Data that (can) distinguish one object from another. Aka properties, member variables, instance variables
public string FirstName {get; set;}


Behavior
Instance methods (object methods) are methods that run on an object. They represent the object’s abilities. They can also change the object’s properties.



Publicly visible
A class/constructor/property/method is public and can be used from any other project in the same VS solution - see unit tests.
public


Private
Private data or methods that only the class itself needs to fulfill its tasks.
private


Read-only properties
Only read access to an object’s properties is publicly allowed. Setting or changing the property may only happen from inside the class itself.
public string FirstName {get; private set;}


field keyword
Since C# 14: inside a property accessor, field is the backing field the compiler creates. Lets you add a check to an auto property without declaring the field yourself.
public int? ZipCode { get; set { if (...) field = value; } }


Computed properties
Only a get accessor is defined for the property. The property’s value can’t be set because it is freshly computed on every access.
public int Age {get { ... } }


Class methods
Can only be invoked on the class name, not on object instances. Examples: Console.WriteLine(), CsvImporter.ReadCsvFile()
static methods of a class


Static field
Exists once for the whole class and is shared by all objects.
private static int _nextId;


Constant
Value fixed in the code at compile time; belongs to the class and is used via the class name.
public const int MaxSteps = 20;


Read-only field
Set at the declaration or in the constructor, never changed afterwards. For arrays and objects only the reference is fixed, not the contents.
private readonly Horse[] _horses;
